title: Thirty-Seven Years in Room Four and the Constitutional Frontiers of Dying with Dignity
hook: A historic constitutional judgment recognized passive euthanasia and affirmed that the fundamental right to life embraces a dignified death.

facts.label: Court
facts.value: Supreme Court of India (Criminal Original and Constitutional Jurisdictions)

facts.label: Medical Condition
facts.value: Permanent vegetative state resulting from irreversible hypoxic-ischemic brain damage

facts.label: Duration of Hospital Care
facts.value: Over thirty-seven continuous years of bedridden institutional care without a single bedsore

facts.label: Legal Question
facts.value: Whether life support and artificial nutrition may be withdrawn from an incompetent patient under passive euthanasia

summary: Following a brutal sexual assault and strangulation in a public hospital basement, a dedicated staff nurse suffered catastrophic cerebral hypoxia that extinguished her cognitive faculties while leaving her autonomic brainstem intact. For nearly four decades, her fellow hospital nurses transformed a small hospital room into a sanctuary of continuous care, attending to her bodily needs with extraordinary devotion so that she never developed a single bedsore or systemic infection.

A social activist and author filed a public interest writ petition before the Supreme Court claiming to act as the patient's next friend, seeking judicial permission to withdraw artificial hydration and feeding to bring an end to her prolonged vegetative existence. The hospital nursing staff fiercely opposed the petition, asserting that the patient was not in unbearable pain, reacted to voices and music, and had become an adopted member of their institutional family.

The Supreme Court dismissed the plea to terminate life-sustaining measures, holding that the hospital staff who cared for the patient constituted her true next friend under the protective doctrine of the state. However, the bench made historic constitutional law by legalizing passive euthanasia across the nation, laying down stringent procedural safeguards requiring High Court approval and independent medical panels before life-support systems can be lawfully withdrawn from terminally ill patients.

timeline.title: Tragic Assault
timeline.text: A hospital ward nurse suffers irreversible brain damage following a brutal assault and asphyxiation in a medical basement.

timeline.title: Public Interest Petition
timeline.text: A writer and activist petitions the Supreme Court seeking permission to withdraw life-sustaining measures.

timeline.title: Medical Panel Report
timeline.text: A court-appointed board of specialists submits a clinical evaluation confirming permanent vegetative condition without acute suffering.

timeline.title: Historic Euthanasia Ruling
timeline.text: The Supreme Court legalizes passive euthanasia with judicial safeguards but rejects the petition to stop feeding the nurse.

timeline.title: Living Wills Recognized
timeline.text: A five-judge Constitution Bench reaffirms passive euthanasia and recognizes advance medical directives.

judgment.outcome: Writ petition dismissed regarding the specific patient; passive euthanasia recognized as legally permissible in India subject to strict High Court approval procedures and multi-disciplinary medical board evaluations.
points: Active euthanasia involving the administration of lethal substances remains unlawful and constitutes culpable homicide or murder.
Passive euthanasia involving the withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment or artificial hydration from a permanently vegetative patient is legally permissible.
The ultimate decision to withdraw life support requires formal approval from the relevant High Court exercising constitutional parens patriae authority.
Hospital nursing staff who provided lifelong daily care, rather than external petitioners, qualify as the patient's genuine next friend.

principles.name: Doctrine of Parens Patriae
principles.meaning: The state and the courts hold an inherent paternal duty to protect the legal rights and well-being of citizens unable to care for themselves.
principles.inThisCase: The court held that judges must exercise ultimate supervisory jurisdiction to ensure that decisions to withdraw life support reflect the patient's best interests.

principles.name: Distinction Between Active and Passive Euthanasia
principles.meaning: Active euthanasia entails taking positive physical steps to end life, whereas passive euthanasia consists of withholding artificial measures to let nature take its course.
principles.inThisCase: The bench held that while positive acts causing death are penal offenses, allowing a dying patient to die naturally when recovery is impossible is lawful.

principles.name: Right to Die with Dignity as Facet of Life
principles.meaning: The constitutional right to life under Article 21 encompasses living and dying with human dignity rather than enduring prolonged, futile bodily degradation.
principles.inThisCase: The court ruled that keeping a hopelessly vegetative body artificially animated against nature violates the intrinsic dignity protected by the Constitution.

takeaways: Passive euthanasia is constitutionally recognized in India, enabling the humane withdrawal of futile life-support systems.
Withdrawal of artificial life-sustaining treatment requires strict clearance from a High Court bench and specialized medical boards.
Lifelong institutional caregivers hold primary legal status as next friends over outside parties seeking to determine patient welfare.

new.title: Attempt to commit suicide to compel or restrain exercise of lawful power

lawMapping.change: Decriminalized general suicide attempts, restricting penal liability exclusively to attempts made to coerce public servants from performing duties.
Re-enacted penal provisions punishing any individual who aids or instigates another person to commit suicide.
Re-enacted comprehensive penal sanctions punishing deliberate physical assaults endangering human life.

lawNote: The constitutional review evaluated the boundaries of life and death under Article 21 and the Indian Penal Code, 1860. Modern statutory developments under the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 and the Bharatiya Sanhitas have transformed the penal treatment of suicide and medical decision-making.

social.hook: Can a court order doctors to stop feeding a bedridden patient who cannot speak for herself?
social.script: Can a court order doctors to stop feeding a bedridden patient who cannot speak for herself? For nearly four decades, a young nurse remained in a hospital room in an irreversible vegetative state after a brutal assault. Her devoted fellow nurses cared for her without a single bedsore, treating her as family. When an author petitioned the Supreme Court to withdraw artificial feeding and let her die, the country faced an agonizing moral dilemma. The judges refused to end her care, but made history by legalizing passive euthanasia nationwide. You be the judge. Full case notes are on the Courtroom Chronicles website.

carousel.heading: The Moral Dilemma
carousel.text: An author asked the Supreme Court to stop tube feeding and let her die peacefully, sparking national ethical debate.

carousel.heading: Why It Matters
carousel.text: The ruling affirmed that human life includes the right to die with dignity, opening the door for advance medical directives.
